title: Why don't clouds fall out of the sky?
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature

explain.say: A cloud can hold hundreds of tonnes of water, yet it floats. The secret is that the water is split into billions of tiny droplets, each only about 0.02 millimetres across.

draw.text: Why don't clouds fall out of the sky?

explain.say: Gravity does pull on every droplet. But a tiny droplet has a lot of surface for its weight, so air resistance almost cancels gravity and it sinks only about a centimetre each second.

Clouds also form in rising air, and an updraft of just a few centimetres per second is enough to hold the droplets up, or even carry them higher. Droplets that sink into drier air below simply evaporate.
Meanwhile the wind carries the whole cloud along. Only when droplets grow into raindrops about a hundred times wider are they heavy enough to fall through the rising air as rain.

faq.a: Cloud droplets are so tiny that air resistance nearly balances their weight, so they drift down only about a centimetre a second. Gentle rising air easily holds them up.

Not the droplets; water is about 800 times denser than air. But a cloud is mostly air with a little water spread through it, and the damp air in a cloud can be slightly lighter than the drier air around it.
asks: Is a cloud heavier than air?

faq.a: Rising air currents, called updrafts, push up on the tiny droplets, and air resistance slows their fall. Together these keep the cloud aloft.
asks: What keeps clouds in the sky?

faq.a: Clouds are carried by the wind. High clouds often move faster than low ones, because winds are usually stronger higher up.

faq.q: When does a cloud let the water fall?
faq.a: When its droplets join into drops big enough that their weight beats air resistance and the rising air. Then they fall as rain, or as snow if it is cold enough.
asks: Why does a cloud start raining?

facts: Water is about 800 times denser than air at sea level.
A cloud droplet falls at only about 1 centimetre per second in still air, while a raindrop falls at several metres per second.
